newsitem.title: TANZANIA: African countries said to ease Burundi blockade.
newsitem.headline: African countries said to ease Burundi blockade.

text.p: Officials of seven African countries have agreed to ease sanctions imposed on Burundi after the coup there to allow humanitarian aid to reach refugees, conference sources said on Sunday.

But their meeting in Arusha, Tanzania, ended on Saturday with no apparent response to a plea from Burundi's military ruler, Major Pierre Buyoya, for the full lifting of sanctions imposed after the July 25 coup that brought him to power.
The sources said the meeting approved a partial easing of the trade ban to allow movement of humanitarian supplies to refugees in Burundi, but there was no formal statement.

They said the meeting also agreed that essential supplies, including fuel, could be moved to diplomats and other foreign organisations in Burundi, who would also be able to travel in and out of the country.
Fuel supplies in landlocked Burundi have been hard hit by the sanctions. Other imported goods are fast running out.

Tanzania, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, Zaire and Zambia, the countries whose officials met in Arusha, have banned surface and air traffic with Burundi to back their demand for restoration of democratic rule.
Buyoya said on Saturday in Bujumbura that Tanzanian mediator and former president Julius Nyerere had agreed to work for a regional summit in the near future to review the sanctions issue.
He spoke after meeting Nyerere in Musoma, western Tanzania.

"President Nyerere agreed to work on a summit of the heads of state of the region in the coming days in order to review the situation and maybe Burundi will be represented in the summit," Buyoya said at a news conference on his return from Musoma.

Buyoya said he planned to reconstitute the National Assembly soon, but urged foreigners not to interfere between his government and the main Hutu rebel group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
"We are going to talk to armed groups, but we ask our partners not to dictate to us how to do it or when to do it," he said.
The meeting with Nyerere was part of contacts between Burundi and neighbouring states held with a view to securing a relaxation of the sanctions, Buyoya said.
About 150,000 people have died in Burundi since 1993, when the country's first democratically elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted army coup.
